ai:rag-pipeline-design.prompt: A user asks a RAG chatbot about an internal policy and gets a confidently wrong answer. Where should you look first to find the cause?
options: Trace the single bad answer: was the right passage retrieved at all, did it make the top-k after reranking, and was it actually in the final prompt
Immediately switch to a bigger, more expensive LLM
Immediately lower the retrieval top-k to reduce noise
Assume it is a prompt-wording issue and rewrite the system prompt
ai:rag-pipeline-design.explanation: Retrieval, reranking and generation each have distinct failure modes that all look like "the answer is wrong" from the outside. Tracing one example through the pipeline tells you which stage actually failed, so you fix the right thing instead of guessing.

ai:rag-pipeline-design.prompt: Why can a reranker improve answer quality even when the embedding model and index are unchanged?
options: A cross-encoder reranker scores the question and each candidate passage together, which is more precise than comparing two independently computed vectors
Rerankers add new documents to the index that the embedding model missed
Rerankers replace the need for chunking entirely
Rerankers always run before retrieval, not after
ai:rag-pipeline-design.explanation: A dense retriever compares a precomputed query vector to precomputed document vectors (fast but approximate). A cross-encoder reranker reads the query and a candidate together in one forward pass, trading speed for precision, so it is used only on a shortlist retrieval already narrowed down.

ai:rag-pipeline-design.prompt: A knowledge base chunk reads only "It is processed within 14 days." What problem does this illustrate?
options: The pronoun problem: a chunk embedded in isolation loses the context (what "it" refers to) needed to retrieve or use it correctly
A tokenizer bug that drops pronouns
A sign that the chunk is too large, not too small
A reranking failure
ai:rag-pipeline-design.explanation: Chunks lose surrounding context. Fixes include prepending heading paths/titles, contextual retrieval (an LLM writes a short situating context per chunk), or late chunking (encoding the whole document before splitting).

ai:rag-pipeline-design.prompt: Why does hybrid retrieval (dense vectors plus BM25/keyword search) matter for a question like "what does error code XR-2041-B mean"?
options: Embedding models are trained on semantic, paraphrase-style pairs and are comparatively weak at exact identifiers; a keyword index catches the literal code reliably
BM25 is always more accurate than dense retrieval for every query type
Dense retrieval cannot index short documents
Hybrid retrieval is only needed when the corpus has no headings
ai:rag-pipeline-design.explanation: Dense embeddings capture "aboutness" well but can treat an exact product code as just another token sequence with no special weight. A keyword/BM25 index, fused with dense results (e.g. reciprocal rank fusion), recovers exact-match cases the embedding model alone would miss.

ai:rag-pipeline-design.prompt: In the diagram for this case, what happens between "Fuse candidates (RRF)" and "Build prompt with top passages"?
options: Rerank (cross-encoder)
Embed question
Parse and chunk
Keyword index (BM25)
ai:rag-pipeline-design.explanation: After fusing the vector and keyword candidate lists, a cross-encoder reranker narrows the wide candidate set down to the small number of passages that actually go in the LLM's prompt.

ai:rag-pipeline-design.prompt: A RAG system retrieves the correct passage at rank 1 but the generated answer still contradicts it. Which stage is most likely at fault?
options: Generation or grounding: the passage was retrieved and in the prompt, but the model ignored or misread it
Retrieval: the embedding model needs replacing
Chunking: the chunks are too small
The vector index needs re-indexing
ai:rag-pipeline-design.explanation: If the right passage made it into the prompt and the answer still contradicts it, the failure is in generation (the model didn't use the context faithfully) or in how the prompt presents the evidence, not in retrieval.

ai:rag-pipeline-design.prompt: Why should a retrieval-augmented system re-chunk and re-embed a document by content hash rather than on a fixed schedule?
options: So unchanged chunks are skipped and only edited content is re-embedded, keeping ingestion idempotent and cheap
Because embedding APIs require a hash in every request
Because content hashes are required for vector databases to boot
Because a fixed schedule is always cheaper than hashing
ai:rag-pipeline-design.explanation: Keying re-embedding by a content hash means re-running ingestion is a no-op for unchanged text and only pays the embedding cost for chunks that actually changed, which is both cheaper and safer than a blind scheduled re-embed.

ai:rag-pipeline-design.prompt: A document is deleted from the knowledge base, but the chatbot keeps citing a policy from it weeks later. What was most likely missed?
options: Deleting the document's chunks from the index when the source document is removed
Running a reranker on every query
Increasing the chunk overlap percentage
Adding a keyword index
ai:rag-pipeline-design.explanation: Orphaned chunks of deleted or edited documents are a common, quiet source of stale or wrong answers. Deletes and permission changes need to propagate to the index just like new content does.

ai:rag-pipeline-design.prompt: Which two things does a complete RAG evaluation need, beyond "it feels right when I try a few questions"?
options: A retrieval metric (e.g. recall@k against labelled question-passage pairs) and a generation metric (faithfulness/groundedness and relevance)
Only a generation metric, since retrieval cannot be measured objectively
Only a retrieval metric, since a good retriever guarantees a good answer
A single end-to-end accuracy number with no breakdown
ai:rag-pipeline-design.explanation: Retrieval and generation fail independently, so each needs its own measurement: did the right passage get retrieved at all, and did the model's answer actually use it faithfully and answer the question. Conflating the two hides which stage to fix.

ai:rag-pipeline-design.prompt: True or false: a chunk size that works well for one embedding model is guaranteed to work equally well for a different embedding model.
options: True
False
ai:rag-pipeline-design.explanation: Chunking and embedding choices interact: input token limits, pooling strategy and what the model was contrastively trained on all differ by model, so a chunk size should be re-validated against a retrieval eval whenever the embedding model changes.

ai:rag-pipeline-design.prompt: Why is parent-child (small-to-big) retrieval used instead of just picking one chunk size?
options: It lets you match precisely on small child chunks while returning the larger parent section for context, resolving the small-vs-large chunk trade-off instead of compromising on one size
It removes the need for an embedding model entirely
It is required by every vector database by default
It eliminates the need for a reranker
ai:rag-pipeline-design.explanation: Small chunks give sharp, precise matches but can split an answer across chunks; large chunks keep context together but dilute the embedding across several topics. Parent-child retrieval decouples the unit you match on from the unit you return to the LLM.

ai:rag-pipeline-design.prompt: Select every statement below that is a real risk of raising retrieval top-k without adding a reranker.
options: More irrelevant passages compete for space in the prompt, pushing out the truly relevant ones
Prompt cost and latency increase because more text is sent to the LLM
The embedding model itself becomes slower to query
The vector index loses previously indexed documents
ai:rag-pipeline-design.explanation: A bigger top-k without reranking dilutes the prompt with lower-quality matches and costs more tokens and latency. It does not slow the embedding model or delete indexed documents; a reranker is the usual fix to raise top-k safely.

ai:rag-pipeline-design.prompt: An interviewer asks: "How would you decide the chunk size, rather than guessing a round number?" What is the strongest answer?
options: Build a small labelled retrieval eval (questions with their correct passage) first, then compare chunk sizes by recall@k and iterate on real numbers
Always use 512 tokens because most embedding models default to it
Ask the LLM what chunk size it prefers
Pick the largest size the embedding model allows, since more context is always better
ai:rag-pipeline-design.explanation: Chunk size is an empirical decision, not a rule of thumb: a retrieval eval with real questions and labelled correct passages lets you measure recall at different chunk sizes and change one variable at a time.

ai:rag-pipeline-design.prompt: What does reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) do in a hybrid retrieval pipeline?
options: Combines the ranked candidate lists from the dense and keyword retrievers into one merged ranking, favouring documents that rank well in either list
Reduces the dimensionality of the embedding vectors
Retrains the embedding model on both dense and sparse signals
Removes duplicate chunks from the vector index
ai:rag-pipeline-design.explanation: RRF is a simple, effective way to merge two independently ranked lists (vector and keyword) into one fused ranking without needing to calibrate the two systems' raw scores against each other.

ai:rag-pipeline-design.prompt: Why is "faithfulness" (or groundedness) scored separately from "relevance" when evaluating RAG generations?
options: An answer can be relevant to the question but unfaithful to the retrieved sources (hallucinated or extrapolated), or faithful but fail to actually answer what was asked, so each needs its own check
Faithfulness and relevance always move together, so only one needs to be measured
Relevance can only be measured by a human, never automatically
Faithfulness is only relevant for coding assistants, not RAG
ai:rag-pipeline-design.explanation: A RAG answer can go wrong in two independent ways: it can drift from what the sources actually say (unfaithful) or correctly reflect the sources while missing the point of the question (irrelevant). Scoring both catches failures the other would miss.

ai:rag-pipeline-design.prompt: A support bot's RAG system works well for most questions but consistently fails on questions that reference "the policy mentioned above" within a long document. What technique addresses this most directly?
options: Contextual retrieval or late chunking, so each chunk's vector carries the surrounding context it needs to be found and understood on its own
Switching from cosine similarity to Euclidean distance
Increasing the LLM's temperature
Removing the reranker
ai:rag-pipeline-design.explanation: Implicit references ("above", "it", "this plan") are exactly what chunk-level embeddings struggle with. Contextual retrieval prepends an LLM-written situating sentence per chunk; late chunking embeds the whole document first so token vectors already reflect context.

ai:rag-pipeline-design.prompt: What is a reasonable first response to "recall looks great in testing but users complain production answers are wrong"?
options: Suspect the production corpus, freshness or query distribution differs from the eval set, and build an eval slice from real production questions and documents to find the gap
Assume the eval numbers were fabricated and discard them
Immediately retrain the embedding model from scratch
Disable retrieval and answer from the model's parametric knowledge instead
ai:rag-pipeline-design.explanation: A strong eval score on a curated test set does not guarantee production performance if real queries, document freshness, or edge cases differ. The fix is to extend the eval with real production traces, not to throw out retrieval.

ai:rag-pipeline-design.prompt: The case's reading on contextual retrieval is from which source?
options: Anthropic
A LeetCode discussion thread
The Postgres documentation
A Reddit post
ai:rag-pipeline-design.explanation: The first reading links to Anthropic's write-up on contextual retrieval, the ingestion-time technique of prepending an LLM-generated context sentence to each chunk before embedding and indexing.

ai:rag-pipeline-design.prompt: Why would you prefer updating only the chunks whose content actually changed in a document, rather than re-embedding the whole document on every edit?
options: It avoids unnecessary embedding API cost and keeps ingestion idempotent and fast for large, frequently-edited corpora
Partial re-embedding is required by every embedding provider's terms of service
Whole-document re-embedding is technically impossible
It increases retrieval recall automatically
ai:rag-pipeline-design.explanation: Content-hash-keyed, chunk-level re-embedding is purely an efficiency and operability concern for large or frequently changing corpora; it does not by itself change what gets retrieved, just how cheaply the index stays current.

ai:rag-pipeline-design.prompt: A candidate claims "RAG means the LLM searches the internet before answering." What is the more accurate description you would give in an interview?
options: RAG retrieves relevant passages from your own indexed corpus (not a live web search) and includes them in the prompt so the model can ground its answer in them
RAG is a fine-tuning technique that changes the model's weights
RAG only works with proprietary, closed-source models
RAG replaces the need for a prompt entirely
ai:rag-pipeline-design.explanation: Retrieval-augmented generation is about retrieving from a chosen, usually private, indexed knowledge source at query time and feeding the results into the prompt; it is unrelated to live web browsing and does not change the model's weights.
